Diagnostician:

[THOUGHT]  
This 53-year-old male presents with isolated, persistent fatigue and laboratory-confirmed iron deficiency (low serum iron, low ferritin, low iron saturation, high TIBC) — classic biochemical signature of iron deficiency. Critically, he has concomitant thrombocytosis (platelets 700,000/μL), which in the setting of iron deficiency is almost always *reactive* (i.e., secondary thrombocytosis), not clonal — especially given absence of other features of myeloproliferative neoplasm (e.g., leukocytosis, splenomegaly, JAK2 mutation, abnormal peripheral smear, or constitutional symptoms).  

The absence of overt GI symptoms, NSAID use, or acute bleeding does *not* exclude significant gastrointestinal pathology: colorectal cancer, gastric adenocarcinoma, or celiac disease often present insidiously in this demographic with isolated fatigue and iron deficiency anemia (IDA). Per ACG and AGA guidelines, unexplained IDA in men ≥50 years mandates bidirectional endoscopy regardless of FIT result — because FIT has suboptimal sensitivity for proximal lesions and non-bleeding malignancies (e.g., early gastric cancer, sessile serrated lesions). Thrombocytosis here is a red herring unless proven otherwise; it reinforces, rather than distracts from, the diagnosis of reactive IDA — since reactive thrombocytosis is common in IDA (up to 30–40% of cases) and resolves with iron repletion.  

No evidence supports primary hematologic malignancy (e.g., essential thrombocythemia): no leukoerythroblastic changes, no splenomegaly, no thrombotic/hemorrhagic history, and ferritin is low — which is incompatible with clonal thrombocytosis (where ferritin is typically normal or elevated). Likewise, chronic inflammation or infection is unlikely without fever, elevated CRP/ESR, or other systemic signs — and iron studies show *true* iron deficiency (low ferritin), not anemia of chronic disease (which features high/normal ferritin).  

Thus, the unifying diagnosis explaining *all* findings — fatigue, iron deficiency, reactive thrombocytosis — is **iron deficiency anemia due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss**, most likely from a premalignant or malignant lesion (e.g., colorectal adenocarcinoma or advanced adenoma), pending endoscopic confirmation.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Iron deficiency anemia due to occult gastrointestinal malignancy
